                                     PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                              §
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                     §
                                                                        OF TEXAS
 THE ERCOT REGION                                  §

           VISTRA CORPORATE SERVICES COMPANY LLC’S COMMENTS

        Vistra Corporate Services Company LLC (Vistra) files these Comments in response to the
Proposal for Publication (PFP or Proposed Rule(s)) to amend 16 Texas Admin. Code
(TAC) §§ 25.192 and 25.193, and adopt new 16 TAC § 25.252. This rulemaking is to implement
Section 6 of Senate Bill 6 (SB6) adopted during the 89th Texas Legislative Session (R.S.),
requiring the Commission to evaluate whether the existing methodology used to charge wholesale
transmission   costs   to   distribution   providers   under   Public   Utility   Regulatory Act
(PURA) § 35.004(d) continues to appropriately assign costs for transmission investment. The
Proposed Rule established a comment deadline of August 11, 2026, therefore these comments are
timely filed. As requested, the executive summary is included in a separate attachment at the end
of the comments. In addition, Vistra has attached as an appendix a full redline of the Proposed
Rule.

                                I.     GENERAL COMMENTS

        Vistra supports the Commission’s efforts to implement the Legislature’s directives in this
rulemaking and shares in the goal of supporting economic development in Texas while protecting
against inappropriate cost shifting between and within rate classes. In Project No. 58484, Vistra
established two core principles: (1) the transmission cost allocation methodology must be fair to
all customers; and, at the same time, (2) minimize any interference with the ERCOT wholesale
market while keeping TSPs whole for prudently incurred investments.

        The Proposed Rules are likely to broadly satisfy the second criterion. While the use of any
coincident peak-based cost allocation design will allow for some zero-sum behavior, the Proposed
Rule’s 12 Coincident Peak (12CP) proposed framework should dilute the non-market load
behavioral incentive that has historically distorted wholesale electricity market price formation




Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                           Page 1 of 16
                                                                                                       001
 relative to the status quo, all else equal. Furthermore, the minimum billing demand approach for
new large loads should further temper this dynamic.

       Therefore, it is the first criterion regarding fairness that broadly guides Vistra’s comments.
Vistra recognizes that there will likely be many comments from stakeholders regarding the
objective and subjective fairness of the Proposed Rules. Vistra looks forward to reviewing
stakeholder comments through this lens and respectfully reserves the right to respond to other
stakeholders’ recommendations as warranted. In these comments, Vistra offers a narrow focus on
one small subset of customers that co-locate with generation resources.

       The Proposed Rule structure appears to reflect the most common large load interconnection
approach, wherein the large load directly interconnects to the bulk power system, taking retail
electric delivery service from a Distribution Service Provider (DSP), typically at transmission
voltage. However, when the large load interconnects in a manner that is netted with a co-located
generation resource, there are added complexities such as self-service and transmission planning
considerations (e.g., co-located net metering arrangements with existing generation and co-located
Withdrawal Limited Private Use Networks (WLPUNs) in Batch Zero may require little or no
additional transmission infrastructure, and may operate under strong net load control requirements
that limit or preclude their utilization of the transmission system). To address these scenarios,
Vistra recommends that (1) the Proposed Rules apply only to large loads that take retail electric
delivery service; and (2) the Minimum Billing Demand rule formulation should include a
multiplier factor for the contracted peak demand and non-coincident peak demand options that
reflect the Annual Net Load Ratio (ANLR) of large loads co-located with a generation resource
(and their associated transmission efficiencies).

                     II.     RESPONSES TO PREAMBLE QUESTIONS

   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
      be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
      different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       Vistra supports a minimum billing demand framework that reflects cost causation and
accounts for the transmission planning impacts of large load customers to appropriately protect
residential and other rate classes. Vistra does not oppose different minimum billing demand values



Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                            Page 2 of 16
                                                                                                        002
 for large load customers with materially different contracted peak demands or non-coincident peak
(NCP) demands if the associated proposed structure would fairly meet those objectives. Any tier
thresholds and minimum billing demand ratios should be supported by evidence demonstrating
that customers in different size categories impose materially different transmission planning and
cost recovery risks.

        Vistra does support the Commission including a differentiated minimum billing demand
charge for Net Metering Arrangements of large loads netted with a generator. This kind of co-
location of load and generation is transmission-efficient, because the transmission system can be
planned to account for the offsetting production and consumption. In the case of Net Metering
Arrangements with existing generation resources, the interconnecting transmission infrastructure
already exists and no additional transmission infrastructure may be necessary. Furthermore, if the
site will continue to be a net generator there may be no retail electric delivery service to the large
load at all.

        The Commission should either establish a separate minimum billing demand approach for
Net Metering Arrangements that appropriately accounts for their unique characteristics, or modify
its proposed minimum demand billing rules to scale their applicability in a manner that
appropriately reflects the full spectrum of transmission-efficient grid dynamics that Net Metering
Arrangements support. In these comments, Vistra has proposed that (1) the Proposed Rules apply
only to large loads that take retail electric delivery service; and (2) the Minimum Billing Demand
rule formulation should include a multiplier factor for the contracted peak demand and non-
coincident peak demand options that reflect the Annual Net Load Ratio (ANLR) of large loads co-
located with a generation resource (and their associated transmission efficiencies).


    2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
          a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
          b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
          c. extended to a longer time period?

        Vistra reads the Commission’s intent to be that the transmission infrastructure built to
support large loads will be meaningfully financially supported by the large loads appropriately
commensurate with their impacts on the transmission system. That could be achieved by
maintaining the large load minimum billing demand for a fixed period or by reducing it over time,


Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                             Page 3 of 16
                                                                                                         003
 with or without collateralization – but there are trade-offs to consider. The purpose of the minimum
billing demand is to ensure that large load customers contribute to the recovery of transmission
costs associated with the infrastructure built to serve them and to mitigate the risk that stranded
transmission investments are shifted to other customers. Transmission assets have a very long life
in rate base, though the rate impact of their depreciation schedule may be greatest early in their
lifespan since even straight line depreciation shrinks the rate base – and associated cost of capital
recovery – over time (all else equal).

       A fixed term for a minimum billing demand value may provide relative administrative
simplicity, customer certainty, and alignment between transmission planning assumptions, cost
recovery, and customer responsibility. However, it may under-recover in early years when un-
depreciated rate base is higher, which is offset by future over-recovery. This may warrant
consideration of some financial security to achieve the Commission’s objective of protecting
against potential cost-shifting.

       A declining term for a minimum billing demand value may most closely align with the
depreciated rate base and associated cost of capital reflected in transmission rates, and in turn
should reduce under-recovery risks, which may not warrant as much financial security. However,
this approach may be misaligned with the load’s business development plans – putting the highest
cost on the customer just as their business opens. And, a phased reduction that does not follow the
underlying depreciation could also weaken the protection against stranded costs while reducing
certainty regarding recovery of transmission investments that were planned and constructed based
on the customer's requested capacity.

       Vistra does not oppose the proposed 20-year term as a reasonable starting point that should
appropriately balance the interests of large load customers, transmission providers, and other
ratepayers. To the extent the Commission determines that transmission assets supporting large load
customers have material cost recovery horizons extending beyond that timeframe that are not
appropriately allocated through normal means or that other network benefits offset the need for
long-term direct cost assignment to large loads, a different period may be justifiable.


   3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
      lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
      load minimum billing demand:


Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                             Page 4 of 16
                                                                                                         004
            a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
              is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum
              NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
              in phases over the years, and how?
           b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
              load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
              customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
              year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
              weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
              over the years, and how?

       Contracted peak demand represents the highest potential demand anticipated at a site, so
relying on contracted peak demand would virtually guarantee that contracted peak demand
becomes the de facto billing determinant. Note that other loads are not billed based on the
theoretical maximum – because that theoretical, non-coincident demand may not always align with
the drivers of transmission growth. While it is important that the transmission cost allocation
mechanism adopted in this rulemaking ensures that large loads contribute meaningfully and
commensurate with their impacts on the transmission system, that objective can still be achieved
without setting the minimum demand charge strictly at the contracted peak demand.

       The Commission should, at a minimum, include differentiated minimum billing demand
charges for Net Metering Arrangements of large loads netted with a generation resource. This kind
of co-location of load and generation is transmission-efficient, because the transmission system
can be planned to account for the offsetting production and consumption. In the case of Net
Metering Arrangements with existing generation resources, the interconnecting transmission
infrastructure already exists and no additional transmission infrastructure may even be necessary.
Furthermore, if the site will continue to be a net generator there may be no retail electric delivery
service to the large load at all. Therefore, the Commission should either establish a separate
minimum billing demand approach for Net Metering Arrangements that appropriately accounts for
their unique characteristics, or modify its proposed minimum demand billing rules to scale their
applicability in a manner that appropriately reflects the full spectrum of transmission-efficient grid
dynamics that Net Metering Arrangements support.

       In these comments, Vistra has proposed that (1) the Proposed Rules apply only to large
loads that take retail electric delivery service; and (2) the Minimum Billing Demand rule
formulation should include a multiplier factor for the contracted peak demand and non-coincident


Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                             Page 5 of 16
                                                                                                         005
 peak demand options that reflect the Annual Net Load Ratio (ANLR) of large loads co-located
with a generation resource (and their associated transmission efficiencies).

       Regarding the sub-questions about ratcheting vs. weighted averaging and adjustments over
time, Vistra recommends that the Commission prioritize alignment with cost causation principles
that appropriately protect residential and other rate classes from potential cost shifting, as well as
administrative ease of implementation and operation. From that standpoint, a ratchet approach
seems more straightforward than a weighted average, but without more detail about a specific
framework Vistra does not have a firm opinion. Regarding the phasing out design features, Vistra
reiterates that if the design risks under-recover in early years when depreciation expense is high
then it may warrant consideration of some financial security to achieve the Commission’s objective
of protecting against potential cost-shifting.


   4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
      an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
      Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
      electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
      cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
      applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
      computational loads?

       Vistra does not oppose separate rate treatment for large computational loads if the
Commission determines that such customers impose materially different transmission planning,
cost recovery, or reliability impacts that justify differentiated treatment. However, any distinction
should be supported by cost-causation principles and objective evidence rather than customer type
alone. Computational loads are not homogeneous, and the transmission impacts of individual
facilities may vary significantly based on net metering/co-location status, load flexibility,
curtailment capability, and other operational characteristics. Accordingly, any separate rate
treatment should be based on demonstrable differences in transmission-related impacts, not solely
on whether a customer qualifies as a data center, cryptocurrency mining facility, or other
computational load. This approach promotes fairness, limits the potential for undue discrimination
among similarly situated customers, and aligns transmission cost recovery with actual system
impacts.




Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                             Page 6 of 16
                                                                                                         006
    5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
      transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
      serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       In the absence of a more detailed framework, Vistra does not have a direct response. The
Commission should focus on maintaining alignment between transmission planning assumptions,
customer responsibility, and transmission cost recovery while protecting against undue cost
shifting among customer classes. While this kind of framework could align with those goals, it is
not necessary to achieve them.

       Vistra notes that the definition of transmission interconnection costs is commonly
understood to mean the costs of the transmission infrastructure necessary to directly interconnect
the load to the broader grid. Broadening that definition to include transmission projects identified
through a batch study may prove complicated, except perhaps where the transmission costs are
demonstrably required to serve needs of only one particular load (though even then, that kind of
assignment can prove tricky over the course of many years as other customers may benefit from
the initial transmission investment beyond the interconnection point for the original load).

       If the Commission pursues a policy that attempts to incorporate certain transmission
upgrades into “interconnection costs,” any such expansion should be based on clear cost-causation
principles and objective criteria demonstrating a direct connection between the load and the
transmission investment. Because many transmission projects identified through batch studies may
also provide broader reliability, economic, or growth-related benefits, having clear and fair
guidelines to distinguish between customer-specific upgrades and projects that provide substantial
system-wide value would be necessary.


   6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
      whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
      how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
      and transmission planning studies?

       If a large load customer is permitted to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
whether the customer has energized or is fully utilizing that capacity, then by definition ERCOT's
transmission planning processes should reflect those reserved transmission commitments in a
transparent and consistent manner. Transmission infrastructure for large loads is planned and



Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                            Page 7 of 16
                                                                                                        007
 constructed based on committed capacity requests (as validated under the pending Commission
rulemaking in Project No. 58481), not solely on actual near-term energy consumption. As a result,
transmission planning studies should recognize reserved transmission capacity that has satisfied
applicable commitment requirements while clearly distinguishing between operating load,
committed future load, and speculative load.

       On the other hand, resource adequacy reports look at the balance of reasonably anticipated
supply of generation in a given season and year to meet reasonably anticipated demand in that
same given season and year. While the same load forecast may underpin both the transmission
planning studies and the resource adequacy studies, the use cases are distinct.

       Consider, for example, a hypothetical 500 MW large load that will ramp up by 100 MW
each year for five years. ERCOT’s transmission planning will want to aim for the full 500 MW at
the end of Year 5, while ensuring the load ramp can be supported along the way – which may mean
having the transmission capability to serve 500 MW as soon as Year 2. On the other hand, a
resource adequacy study will be looking at how much peak load potential exists relative to supply
– and the transmission capability to serve 500 MW in Year 2 has no bearing on that (because there
would only be at most 200 MW load to serve). Therefore, the resource adequacy studies should
limit their view to only what is in the load commissioning plan. It would, however, be helpful for
resource adequacy reports to identify already-energized large load from future committed large
load from energized projects that are ramping up along their load commissioning plan.

       This approach appropriately aligns transmission planning assumptions, reliability
assessments, and cost recovery mechanisms while helping protect other customers from bearing
the costs of transmission investments constructed to serve large load customers. Vistra
recommends that ERCOT and the Commission adopt a framework under which:

       1. Firmly committed large loads with reserved transmission capacity are reflected in
           transmission planning studies.
       2. Resource adequacy reports separately identify operating load and committed future
           load.
       3. Reliability assessments clearly disclose assumptions regarding the timing and
           probability of future load realization.




Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                           Page 8 of 16
                                                                                                       008
        4. Planning processes distinguish between committed and un-committed projects using
             objective criteria.
       5. Transmission planning assumptions remain aligned with transmission cost recovery
             mechanisms and customer responsibility.

                   III.    COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC RULE PROVISIONS

a. The Proposed Rules should be appropriately applied only to large loads that take retail
   electric delivery service from a DSP.

       The Proposed Rules should be clarified to apply only to large loads that take retail electric
delivery service from a DSP. The Proposed Rules appear to reflect the most common large load
interconnection structure, in which a large load directly interconnects to the bulk power system
and takes retail delivery service from a DSP, typically at transmission voltage. That assumption
works in most cases, but may not hold where a large load is co-located with a generation resource
and may remain fully or substantially offset by the net metering arrangement.

       This clarification is consistent with cost-causation principles and is fair because it avoids
applying large load transmission cost responsibility rules to co-located configurations that do not
impose transmission planning and cost recovery impacts that a standalone large load or even
another co-located large load with that intends to consume grid power and in turn take retail
delivery service from a DSP does. This could be a Net Metering Arrangement with an existing
generator that always remains a net generator, or a Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network
(WLPUN) under Batch Zero that has a 0 MW allocation from Batch Zero (i.e., it is not permitted
to withdraw any load from the grid but can consume the output of the generation resource it is co-
located and netted with.

       For that reason, Vistra recommends that the Proposed Rule be revised to distinguish large
loads that actually take retail electric delivery service from those that do not. Conforming changes
should be made throughout the Proposed Rules in 16 TAC §§ 25.192(b)(2), 25.193(d)(1), and
25.252(a):

b. The Minimum Billing Demand formulation should include a multiplier factor for the
   contracted peak demand and non-coincident peak demand options that reflect the
   Annual Net Load Ratio (ANLR) of large loads co-located with a generation resource.

       Vistra recommends that the Minimum Billing Demand formulation include an Annual Net
Load Ratio (ANLR) multiplier for large loads co-located with a generation resource. A co-located
large load that is frequently or overwhelmingly offset by on-site generation does not impose the
same transmission planning profile as a standalone load of the same contracted peak demand or
NCP demand. In particular, Net Metering Arrangements with existing generation and WLPUNs
under Batch Zero may require little or no incremental transmission infrastructure and may operate
under controls that substantially limit net load exposure to the ERCOT system.



Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                          Page 10 of 16
                                                                                                       010
        This approach preserves the Commission’s objective of ensuring meaningful large load
contribution to transmission cost recovery while recognizing the transmission efficiencies created
when generation and load are co-located and netted. While parameters can be tuned, a reasonable
formulation may look something like the following, which is based on the Annual Net Load Ratio
(ANLR), determined by the ratio of ERCOT settlement intervals registering a net load condition
during a twelve (12) month period and the total ERCOT settlement intervals during the same
twelve (12) month period; and applies a scaling multiplier (M) to the ANLR above a de minimis
threshold (Level 1 Limit, L1L), up to a pre-determined threshold ratio upon which the full
Minimum Billing Demand will apply as with a standalone large load (Level 2 Limit, L2L).

       In this example, M = 4, L1L = 0.002, and L2L = 0.2 – meaning that if more than 0.2% of
settlement intervals record a net load, the ANLR factor will rise at four (4) times the net load
interval ratio before jumping to unity (1) at 20%. This should provide a strong transmission-
efficient incentive to align generation and consumption while also ensuring fair transmission cost
causation allocation above a certain threshold. There are many other reasonable configurations.

                                I.     GENERAL COMMENTS

        Vistra supports the Commission's efforts to implement the Legislature's directives in this
rulemaking and shares in the goal of supporting economic development in Texas while protecting
against inappropriate cost shifting between and within rate classes. In Project No. 58484, Vistra
established two core principles: (1) the transmission cost allocation methodology must be fair to
all customers; and, at the same time, (2) minimize any interference with the ERCOT wholesale
market while keeping TSPs whole for prudently incurred investments.

        The Proposed Rules are likely to broadly satisfy the second criterion. While the use of any
coincident peak-based cost allocation design will allow for some zero-sum behavior, the Proposed
Rule's 12 Coincident Peak (12CP) proposed framework should dilute the non-market load
behavioral incentive that has historically distorted wholesale electricity market price formation

 relative to the status quo, all else equal. Furthermore, the minimum billing demand approach for
new large loads should further temper this dynamic.

       Therefore, it is the first criterion regarding fairness that broadly guides Vistra's comments.
Vistra recognizes that there will likely be many comments from stakeholders regarding the
objective and subjective fairness of the Proposed Rules. Vistra looks forward to reviewing
stakeholder comments through this lens and respectfully reserves the right to respond to other

       The Proposed Rule structure appears to reflect the most common large load interconnection
approach, wherein the large load directly interconnects to the bulk power system, taking retail
electric delivery service from a Distribution Service Provider (DSP), typically at transmission
voltage. However, when the large load interconnects in a manner that is netted with a co-located
generation resource, there are added complexities such as self-service and transmission planning
considerations (e.g., co-located net metering arrangements with existing generation and co-located
Withdrawal Limited Private Use Networks (WLPUNs) in Batch Zero may require little or no
additional transmission infrastructure, and may operate under strong net load control requirements
that limit or preclude their utilization of the transmission system). To address these scenarios,
Vistra recommends that (1) the Proposed Rules apply only to large loads that take retail electric
delivery service; and (2) the Minimum Billing Demand rule formulation should include a
multiplier factor for the contracted peak demand and non-coincident peak demand options that
reflect the Annual Net Load Ratio (ANLR) of large loads co-located with a generation resource
(and their associated transmission efficiencies).

       Vistra supports a minimum billing demand framework that reflects cost causation and

residential and other rate classes. Vistra does not oppose different minimum billing demand values

(NCP) demands if the associated proposed structure would fairly meet those objectives. Any tier

that customers in different size categories impose materially different transmission planning and

        Vistra does support the Commission including a differentiated minimum billing demand
charge for Net Metering Arrangements of large loads netted with a generator. This kind of co-

planned to account for the offsetting production and consumption. In the case of Net Metering

        The Commission should either establish a separate minimum billing demand approach for

appropriately reflects the full spectrum of transmission-efficient grid dynamics that Net Metering
Arrangements support. In these comments, Vistra has proposed that (1) the Proposed Rules apply

    2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
          a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
          b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
          c. extended to a longer time period?

        Vistra reads the Commission's intent to be that the transmission infrastructure built to
support large loads will be meaningfully financially supported by the large loads appropriately
commensurate with their impacts on the transmission system. That could be achieved by
maintaining the large load minimum billing demand for a fixed period or by reducing it over time,


Vistra Comments Project 58000                                                             Page 3 of 16
 with or without collateralization - but there are trade-offs to consider. The purpose of the minimum
billing demand is to ensure that large load customers contribute to the recovery of transmission
costs associated with the infrastructure built to serve them and to mitigate the risk that stranded
transmission investments are shifted to other customers. Transmission assets have a very long life
in rate base, though the rate impact of their depreciation schedule may be greatest early in their
lifespan since even straight line depreciation shrinks the rate base - and associated cost of capital
recovery - over time (all else equal).

       A fixed term for a minimum billing demand value may provide relative administrative
simplicity, customer certainty, and alignment between transmission planning assumptions, cost
recovery, and customer responsibility. However, it may under-recover in early years when un-
depreciated rate base is higher, which is offset by future over-recovery. This may warrant
consideration of some financial security to achieve the Commission's objective of protecting
against potential cost-shifting.

       A declining term for a minimum billing demand value may most closely align with the
depreciated rate base and associated cost of capital reflected in transmission rates, and in turn
should reduce under-recovery risks, which may not warrant as much financial security. However,
this approach may be misaligned with the load's business development plans - putting the highest
cost on the customer just as their business opens. And, a phased reduction that does not follow the
underlying depreciation could also weaken the protection against stranded costs while reducing
certainty regarding recovery of transmission investments that were planned and constructed based
on the customer's requested capacity.

        Vistra does not oppose the proposed 20-year term as a reasonable starting point that should
appropriately balance the interests of large load customers, transmission providers, and other
ratepayers. To the extent the Commission determines that transmission assets supporting large load
customers have material cost recovery horizons extending beyond that timeframe that are not
appropriately allocated through normal means or that other network benefits offset the need for
long-term direct cost assignment to large loads, a different period may be justifiable.

mechanism adopted in this rulemaking ensures that large loads contribute meaningfully and
commensurate with their impacts on the transmission system, that obj ective can still be achieved

       The Commission should, at a minimum, include differentiated minimum billing demand
charges for Net Metering Arrangements of large loads netted with a generation resource. This kind
of co-location of load and generation is transmission-efficient, because the transmission system
can be planned to account for the offsetting production and consumption. In the case of Net
Metering Arrangements with existing generation resources, the interconnecting transmission
infrastructure already exi sts and no additional transmission infrastructure may even be necessary.
Furthermore, if the site will continue to be a net generator there may be no retail electric delivery

minimum billing demand approach for Net Metering Arrangements that appropriately accounts for
their unique characteristics, or modify its proposed minimum demand billing rules to scale their

dynamics that Net Metering Arrangements support.

       whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,

       and transmission planning studies?

       If a large load customer is permitted to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
whether the customer has energized or is fully utilizing that capacity, then by definition ERCOT's
transmission planning processes should reflect those reserved transmission commitments in a
transparent and consistent manner. Transmission infrastructure for large loads is planned and

rulemaking in Project No. 58481), not solely on actual near-term energy consumption. As a result,
transmission planning studies should recognize reserved transmission capacity that has satisfied
applicable commitment requirements while clearly distinguishing between operating load,
committed future load, and speculative load.

       On the other hand, resource adequacy reports look at the balance of reasonably anticipated
supply of generation in a given season and year to meet reasonably anticipated demand in that
same given season and year. While the same load forecast may underpin both the transmission
planning studies and the resource adequacy studies, the use cases are distinct.

       Consider, for example, a hypothetical 500 MW large load that will ramp up by 100 MW
each year for five years. ERCOT's transmission planning will want to aim for the full 500 MW at
the end ofYear 5, while ensuring the load ramp can be supported along the way - which may mean
having the transmission capability to serve 500 MW as soon as Year 2. On the other hand, a
resource adequacy study will be looking at how much peak load potential exists relative to supply
- and the transmission capability to serve 500 MW in Year 2 has no bearing on that (because there
would only be at most 200 MW load to serve). Therefore, the resource adequacy studies should
limit their view to only what is in the load commissioning plan. It would, however, be helpful for
resource adequacy reports to identify already-energized large load from future committed large
load from energized proj ects that are ramping up along their load commissioning plan.

assessments, and cost recovery mechanisms while helping protect other customers from bearing
the costs of transmission investments constructed to serve large load customers. Vistra

a. The Proposed Rules should be appropriately applied only to large loads that take retail
   electric delivery service from a DSP.

       The Proposed Rules should be clarified to apply only to large loads that take retail electric
delivery service from a DSP. The Proposed Rules appear to reflect the most common large load
interconnection structure, in which a large load directly interconnects to the bulk power system
and takes retail delivery service from a DSP, typically at transmission voltage. That assumption
works in most cases, but may not hold where a large load is co-located with a generation resource
and may remain fully or substantially offset by the net metering arrangement.

applying large load transmission cost responsibility rules to co-located configurations that do not
impose transmission planning and cost recovery impacts that a standalone large load or even
another co-located large load with that intends to consume grid power and in turn take retail
delivery service from a DSP does. This could be a Net Metering Arrangement with an existing

to withdraw any load from the grid but can consume the output ofthe generation resource it is co-
located and netted with.

loads that actually take retail electric delivery service from those that do not. Conforming changes
